vision:
Aquarella will be an upscale retreat center that offers world-class holistic wellness
and personal transformation retreats for discerning clientele, while still offering
affordable options so that everyone can benefit.
Our mission is to have a wide impact on global consciousness by hosting retreats
for business executives, global thought leaders, and community organizers.
Our space will be filled with such breathtaking beauty that your spirit is renewed
and your soul is filled with inspiration - just by setting foot on the grounds.
We will combine the most advanced tools in self-development with plant medicine
to bring out the highest potential of everyone who arrives.
We will be a global hub for trauma-informed plant medicine work and integration.
Pre and post ceremony care will be woven into the very fabric of our signature
retreats.

Daniel Morningstar
CEO & Founder
Daniel is a serial entrepreneur and polymath. He started his career in the tech sector and ran a successful web development company for over 7 years.
He then managed NYC’s #1 rated youth hostel from 2008 - 2011.
Returning to tech, he built healersource.com, a world-wide online directory for holistic healers.

Project Manager

His current project involves building an aircrete dome home, including a production facility to manufacture the aircrete blocks, in addition to providing training workshops for students interested in building their own domes.

Shelby Sly

Manager

She is also a ceremonialist, Wilderness Therapy Guide, Yoga teacher and Somatic Integration Practitioner, passionate about ecological, individual and collective healing.

Kendal Light
Marketing Director
Kendal is a seasoned creative and marketing strategist with a strong background in digital content creation, community building, and brand development. With years of experience in video production, social media strategy, and high-level content marketing, Kendal has worked alongside wellness leaders, retreat centers, and conscious brands to elevate their presence and drive meaningful engagement.

vision:
A Regenerative Village Blueprint for Human and Ecological Flourishing
Executive Vision
The Living University Network is a regenerative tropical permaculture village designed as a living, economically viable model of ecological autonomy, human development, and replicable community design.
Its purpose is to demonstrate that a village can simultaneously achieve:
•	High economic viability
•	Ecological food autonomy
•	Reduced regional dependency on imported goods
•	A replicable curriculum for regenerative living
•	Architecture informed by material quality, geometry, and bio-energetic principles
•	A holistic educational system integrating health, ecology, and personal development
The project is conceived as a living laboratory where land, community, economy, and education function as one coherent system.
________________________________________
Core Concept
A Living University is an intentional village ecosystem where residents co-create the most supportive possible context for human flourishing.
It is based on three foundational assumptions:
When basic needs are met sustainably and locally, human potential expands.
When individuals are supported physically, emotionally, and socially, collaboration emerges organically.
When ecological systems are designed intelligently, they generate abundance rather than scarcity.
The village becomes both:
•	A functioning regenerative enterprise
•	A teaching and demonstration center
________________________________________
Structural Pillars of the Living University Network
1. Individual Regeneration
Human vitality is the foundation of collective success.
The Living University provides:
•	Access to regenerative health practice and teachings
•	Detoxification and purification protocols
•	High-vitality plant-based food systems
•	Nature immersion, sunlight exposure, and grounding practices
•	Personal development and inner alignment education
The goal is to cultivate resilient, self-aware individuals capable of full participation in community life and leadership.
________________________________________
2. Social Architecture
The village is designed to balance:
•	Private reflection living space
•	Collective participation
•	Shared economic purpose
•	Cultural and educational gatherings

Community design encourages:
•	Belonging without coercion
•	Contribution aligned with individual passion
•	Intergenerational learning
•	Strong social coherence
Instead of rule-dominant systems, the model prioritizes clarity of shared vision and voluntary engagement.
________________________________________
3. Academic & Educational Dimension
The Living University functions as a teaching campus embedded within a real ecosystem.
Curriculum areas include:
•	Tropical permaculture & regenerative agriculture
•	Soil biology and ecosystem restoration
•	Ecological architecture and natural materials
•	Vitality science and lifestyle design
•	Conscious leadership and self-mastery
•	Community governance models
•	Replication frameworks for other regions
The goal is more than abstract theory but rather applied knowledge tested in real conditions.
Graduates and visitors leave with practical knowledge of a replicable system.
________________________________________
4. Economic Model
The economic engine is based on:
•	A very low input economic system
•	Surplus production of high-quality regenerative food and quality day to day products
•	Herbal and value-added transformation products
•	Educational programs and immersive residencies
•	Workshops, certification tracks, and research collaborations
This overproduction strategy allows:
•	Capital generation for expansion
•	Local job creation
•	Impact on local communities to take part on their regional grassroots economic growth
•	Regional reduction in food imports
•	Financial resilience independent of unstable external systems
•	Economic autonomy strengthens community autonomy and abundance.
________________________________________
5. Ecological Systems
The land is developed through advanced tropical permaculture principles to:
•	Regenerate soil fertility
•	Maximize biodiversity
•	Produce food, medicine, and construction materials
•	Increase long-term ecosystem vitality
Design strategies include:
•	Multi-layer food-forestry
•	Supporting soil life abundance
•	Water retention systems
•	Closed-loop nutrient cycles
•	Minimal external inputs
The objective is progressive regeneration, self-sustainability of low maintenance systems.
________________________________________
6. Architectural & Energetic Research
A distinguishing feature of the Living University Network is its research into:
1.	The forgotten science of stone alignment and disposition as to direct Earth’s magnetic network and amplify the aether circulation on the land to generate a high vibrational frequency, supporting soil fertility and living beings vitality.

2.	Natural and mineral-based architecture
•	Geometry and spatial coherence
•	Bio-energetic compatible materials
•	The psychological and physiological effects of built shape-form environments
Architecture becomes both:
•	Functional aesthetic shelter
•	Experimental platform for studying how material quality and form influence well-being through vitalizing frequency generation

3.	Tapping into the Earth’s energy ocean of electric potential to supply local energy needs
•	Patented ‘zero point energy’ suppressed systems have a long unknown history but an existing one
•	Self-sustained communities are the perfect context to introduce these technologies in a private small scale manner

These dimensions open possibilities for partnerships with other groups in ecological architecture, self-energy production and bio-environmental research design.
________________________________________
Regional Impact
The Living University Network aims to:
•	Reduce regional dependency on imported food and others
•	Train replicators to build regional adapted similar villages
•	Create a scalable model adaptable to tropical regions worldwide
•	Serve as a research and demonstration hub for regenerative policy
It is designed to favor networking and replication.
________________________________________
Long-Term Vision
The first village serves as the prototype.
A lot will be learned in its implementation phase alone.
From there, a decentralized network of Living Universities can emerge; each adapted to local climate and culture but grounded in the same principles:
•	Regeneration
•	Autonomy
•	Education
•	Human flourishing
•	Ecological coherence
________________________________________
Why Support This Project
The Living University Network integrates:
•	Regenerative agriculture
•	Ecological economics
•	Educational innovation and practices
•	Efficient community design
•	Applied body / mind / spirit well-being science
•	Radiating extra-community impact
It transforms abstract sustainability ideas into a functioning, measurable, and teachable system.
With appropriate guidance and strategic support, this model can evolve into a reference point for regenerative tropical development.

teamDescription:
françois, house of legault
Francois is a graduate in plant food production with a degree in soil conservation, and his journey of learning has never truly paused. From early on, he has been driven by one central question: how can human settlements integrate harmoniously and intelligently within natural ecosystems? This inquiry has guided years of study and hands-on exploration in tropical horticulture, food forestry, regenerative landscaping, aesthetic design, living architecture, feng shui, geobiology, nutrition, holistic health solutions, and personal development. Over time, these passions converged into a larger vision — innovating a way of living in which human vitality and ecological regeneration are not goals to chase, but natural outcomes of a well-designed system.
Born in Canada, Francois felt a strong call toward the tropics, where biodiversity and regenerative potential are abundant. That calling eventually led him to a beautiful island in Nicaragua, where he is now dedicated to creating spaces designed for life to truly thrive — for the land, for the community, and for the individual.
Justin Lofton
Justin is an experienced community builder with a deep commitment to regenerative living, shared ownership models, and human-centered design. He has spent years studying and implementing systems that integrate sustainability, cooperative economics, food sovereignty, water independence, and intentional governance. His approach blends practical business acumen with a strong understanding of group dynamics, land stewardship, and infrastructure planning. Justin is skilled at translating big vision concepts into executable frameworks, aligning people around shared values, and designing environments that support both individual growth and collective wellbeing.

regenerativePractices:
My regenerative practices are rooted in tropical permaculture design, soil biology restoration (as inspire by the Korean Natural Farming science), whole-systems ecological cycles thinking and the re-introduction of ancient stone work knowledge that favors the harmonization of the meta-physical energy / frequency vibration aspect to the physical living space dynamics. The foundation of my approach is that soil regeneration is the primary lever for restoring ecosystem vitality, long-term productivity and high vitality level food plant production. I prioritize rebuilding soil biome by organic matter input through composting systems, cover cropping, mulching, minimal soil disturbance, and respecting nature’s healing intelligence. Rather than relying on external inputs, I focus on strengthening natural nutrient cycles and increasing microbial life, allowing fertility to compound year after year.
My ecological restoration approach is based on mimicking natural succession patterns. I design multi-layered agroforestry systems that integrate canopy trees, understory species, shrubs, ground covers, and root crops in mutually supportive relationships. Water management is treated as a central design principle, incorporating contour-based earthworks, rainwater harvesting, and infiltration systems to maximize water retention and prevent erosion. Biodiversity is intentionally increased at every stage, not only for productivity but for ecosystem resilience, automatic pest regulation, and habitat restoration.
In tropical contexts especially, I view food production and ecosystem restoration as complementary rather than opposing forces; living polyculture versus monoculture obsolete model. By implementing syntropic and food forest models, degraded land can progressively transition into high-yield, biologically rich systems that produce food, medicine, and building materials while increasing soil organic matter content, microbial density, and over-abundance of nutrient and micro-nutrients by importing long lost complete sea salts. Over time, the objective is to move from extractive production to regenerative abundance, where each season leaves the land more fertile and structurally complex than before, transferring food vitality and nutrient richness to those living being on the land as a direct consequence.
Beyond permaculture land practices, I approach regeneration as an integrated system that includes community design, economic viability, education and self-improvement, basically building a bio-energetically coherent living system where soil vitality, food vitality, human vitality, and spatial energetics are intentionally interlinked.
Ecological restoration becomes durable only when it is socially embedded and economically functional. For this reason, the Living University Network is designed not only to regenerate soil and biodiversity, but to serve as a demonstration and training hub where multi-dimensional regenerative practices are lived, measured, refined, and transmitted to others.
governanceApproach: The Living University Network operates through a stewardship-based governance model combining mission-locked land holding with consent-based decision-making processes. Land is held by a protected entity to ensure ecological and educational continuity, while residents participate through stewardship agreements rather than conventional land ownership. Governance emphasizes shared purpose, distributed responsibility, and principle-based agreements rather than rule-heavy enforcement. Decision-making follows consent processes within functional circles, ensuring both autonomy and alignment. The overall aim is to cultivate a psychologically safe and heart-centered culture where participation arises from intrinsic motivation and shared commitment to regeneration, while maintaining clear structures that preserve operational coherence and long-term stability.
communityEngagement:
The Living University Network is designed not as a closed community, but as a regenerative hub whose vitality naturally radiates outward into the surrounding region. Its primary engagement with the broader community begins with food sovereignty. By producing abundant, high-vitality tropical polyculture crops and value-added products, the project aims to reduce regional dependency on imported food while increasing access to nutrient-dense, biologically rich produce. In this way, ecological restoration and public health improvement move together as complementary outcomes.
Beyond food production, the Living University functions as a demonstration and training center where regenerative agriculture, soil restoration, water management, ecological architecture, and community design are practiced in real conditions. Local farmers, landowners, students, and entrepreneurs are invited to participate in workshops, apprenticeships, and collaborative research initiatives. The objective is to transmit practical knowledge that can be adapted and replicated, progressively expanding regenerative capacity beyond the boundaries of the village itself.
The project also seeks to serve as a bridge between traditional knowledge and modern ecological science. By integrating tropical permaculture, soil microbiology restoration inspired by Korean Natural Farming, and ancient stone and spatial harmonization principles, the Living University fosters a dialogue between ancestral wisdom and contemporary regenerative innovation. This integrative approach honors local cultural context while strengthening long-term ecological resilience.
Economically, the initiative contributes by creating meaningful local employment opportunities, supporting small-scale processing enterprises, and encouraging cooperative distribution networks. Educational programs bring visitors and students into the region, generating responsible eco-conscious activity that benefits surrounding businesses without degrading natural systems.
At a deeper level, the project serves the broader community by modeling an alternative yet practical way of organizing land stewardship, economic exchange, and human collaboration. By demonstrating that ecological regeneration, economic viability, and human wellbeing can reinforce one another, the Living University Network aims to inspire similar initiatives and gradually shift the cultural narrative from extractive development toward regenerative abundance.
timeCommitment: Both Justin and I are completely available to work on the development of the Living University Network project. More participants are expected to join force in the near future.
currentFunding: Describing the vision, objective and functions of the project went alongside building its financial funding structures. As of now, theses structures are in the process of maturing and it is expected that between 3 and 6 months from now, available funds in the range of 5 figures as a start, will become available to initiate its realization.
fundingNeeds:
To move forward responsibly, the Living University Network requires a combination of catalytic capital, technical guidance, and aligned human resources and marketing. The project is designed to develop in phased implementation rather than through large-scale upfront expansion. The initial need is to secure land suited for tropical regenerative development and to establish foundational infrastructure systems including water management, soil regeneration programs, nursery systems, modest residential structures, and basic energy autonomy. Early-stage financing would primarily support land acquisition or long-term stewardship security, ecological master planning, earthworks, initial agroforestry installation, and core operational infrastructure.
Beyond financial capital, strategic resources are equally important. Technical support in legal structuring—particularly in establishing a mission-locked land stewardship entity—will ensure long-term protection and continuity of the project. Guidance in landscaping and community architectural design, regenerative economic modeling, cooperative governance structures, and impact measurement frameworks would strengthen the scalability and credibility of the initiative. Partnerships with institutions, soil scientists, ecological architects, and regenerative agriculture networks would significantly accelerate proper planning and development while maintaining integrity.
Human capital is another essential resource. The first phase requires a small, highly committed founding team with expertise in permaculture implementation, construction, education, operations management, and health-focused regenerative living. As the system matures, the project will progressively integrate apprentices, researchers, and aligned residents who contribute both skill and participation.
Financially, the objective is not perpetual dependency on external funding, but catalytic investment that enables the land to begin generating its own regenerative revenue streams through surplus food production, value-added transformation, and educational programming. The long-term model is designed for economic autonomy, with initial support serving as the ignition point for a self-sustaining ecosystem.
Ultimately, the most valuable resource is alignment: investors, advisors, and collaborators who understand that regeneration requires patience, systems thinking, and long-term stewardship rather than extractive return models. With appropriate catalytic support, the Living University Network can evolve into a functioning prototype capable of replication and global regional impact.
